subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: talking with parents and weighing their concerns [Action]
passage: “Honestly, nobody believes me when I say I didn't argue.” I'm Sabina, and last month a students' march was planned over leaked exam papers. My father, Wasim, said no at once: board prep, crowds, all of it. Instead of shouting, I asked him to tell me every single thing he was scared of. He listed three: getting hurt, losing revision time, being filmed. Then I told him why it mattered, that my cousin lost a whole year because of the leak. Ammi sat down and listened as well. In the end we made a deal. I wouldn't go to the march itself. I'd make posters with the school group at home on Saturday and join the small signature table outside our colony gate. Abbu even carried the posters out. Part of me still wanted to be there, but it felt fair.

qa.q: What three things was Wasim scared of?
qa.a: Getting hurt, losing revision time and being filmed.

qa.q: What might Sabina have been feeling about the deal at the end?
qa.a: Mixed feelings: part of Sabina still wanted to be at the march, but the outcome felt fair because both sides had been heard.

qa.q: What could Sabina try if the parents had refused any kind of taking part, and why?
qa.a: Sabina could write a letter or speak at a school forum from home, since it voices the concern while keeping the family's trust.

qa.q: How does the deal look to Wasim?
qa.a: His worries about safety and revision were listened to and answered, so he could accept a smaller way of taking part and even help carry the posters.

grounding: A teen listens to parents' worries, explains why the issue matters and agrees a limited form of participation.
